title: A Historical and Unifying View of Day-to-Day Traffic Assignment

detail.title: A Historical and Unifying View of Day-to-Day Traffic Assignment
detail.abstract: Day-today (DTD) traffic assignment has produced a wide range of models for explaining how traffic equilibrium emerges. This paper offers a historical and conceptual reconstruction of the field. It traces DTD modeling to three related theoretical fields (learning in games, evolutionary game theory, and stochastic learning theory) and shows how their ideas can be translated across disciplinary boundaries. It also highlights several simple, foundational mechanisms that remain underexplored in the DTD literature. In particular, it derives and analyzes the population-level dynamics of several behavioral models under bandit feedback, in which travelers observe only the outcomes of the routes they choose. The paper's central contribution is a unified view of DTD dynamics, revealing that models built on markedly different microscopic assumptions may nevertheless exhibit substantial similarities in their aggregate convergence paths. Specifically, we show that a broad class of models, despite differing in their behavioral mechanisms (belief-, revision-, or policy-based) and informational assumptions (full information or bandit feedback), either selects the maximum-entropy user equilibrium exactly or is linked to the same benchmark through vanishing-step or vanishing-noise limits. These findings suggest that the apparent diversity of DTD mechanisms may overstate the diversity of their aggregate implications, providing a new basis for model selection and transportation policy benchmarking.

title:
Judgments of Relative Value: 
What would you Offer, and What would you Demand?
affiliations: KU Leuven, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and KU Leuven

detail.title:
Judgments of Relative Value: 
What would you Offer, and What would you Demand?

declarations.ethicsApproval: All studies were approved by the institutional review boards of The University of Pennsylvania or KU Leuven.

detail.abstract: An exchange can be elicited by fixing what a consumer receives and asking what they would offer, or by fixing what they give and asking what they would demand. For example, a consumer could be asked how much they would pay for a fixed number of units of the good or how many units of a good they would demand for paying a fixed dollar value. Across five preregistered studies (N = 3,119), offer elicitations imply higher received-per-given exchange rates than demand elicitations, and this asymmetry widens with magnitude. In both formats, elicited quantities increase sub-proportionally with fixed quantities. This shared response pattern explains the widening asymmetry and conflicts with standard two-sided valuation models. The findings hold across exchanges involving diverse resources, procedural variations, and choices with real monetary or charitable consequences. They also persist when offer and demand elicitations are yoked within participant, showing that the asymmetry cannot be attributed to participant heterogeneity. Together, the findings identify elicitation format as a general feature of exchange judgment, recast resource-specific explanations of time-money asymmetries as potential moderators of a broader effect, and clarify the role of elicitation format in WTP-WTA comparisons.

title: Modeling the Accelerated Development of Civilization
affiliations: Kyiv National Economic University (KNEU)

detail.title: Modeling the Accelerated Development of Civilization
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the intervals between major civilizational and technological transitions have tended to compress over the long run. It synthesizes long-wave theory, the concept of technological structures, and a heuristic periodization based on the reverse Fibonacci sequence. The analysis is explicitly exploratory: historical stage boundaries are treated as approximate transition windows, the Fibonacci specification is not statistically estimated, and the 2008-2029 interval is treated as a prospective test of the model. The paper distinguishes a general acceleration hypothesis from the specific Fibonacci timing rule, treats the proposed continuity between bio-evolution and techno-evolution as a theoretical hypothesis rather than an established law, and identifies 2028-2030 as a falsifiable transition window under the specific model. Competing functional forms, measurement limitations, recent evidence on technological diffusion and artificial intelligence, and implications for strategic planning under potentially shortening technological horizons are discussed.

title: Enhancing Customer Retention: Leveraging Explainable AI, Prescriptive Analytics and Large Language Model
affiliations: Asia e University (AeU), Open University of Sri Lanka

detail.title: Enhancing Customer Retention: Leveraging Explainable AI, Prescriptive Analytics and Large Language Model
detail.abstract:
In the swiftly advancing telecommunications industry, customer retention constitutes a significant business challenge owing to elevated churn rates.  Although predictive analytics is extensively utilised to anticipate customer churn, current research has only minimally investigated the contribution of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in improving the interpretability of these predictions.  Furthermore, the incorporation of prescriptive analytics, which facilitates actionable decisions following predictions, is notably underutilized—especially in relation to the advancing capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). 

This study investigates a comprehensive framework for predictive modelling within fixed network telecommunications, emphasising customer churn prediction.  Employing the IBM Telco dataset, recognised for its significance in the telecommunications industry and adherence to ethical standards, an 80:20 data partition was chosen in accordance with established literature.  The study utilised one-hot and label encoding methods for categorical data representation, supplemented by SMOTEENN for data balancing to attain optimal model configurations.

Min-Max scaling and mutual information-based feature selection were employed to ensure compatibility with various machine learning models.  Algorithms such as Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), Logistic Regression (LR), and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) were assessed, with the SVM model utilising a ‘rbf’ kernel identified as the superior classifier.  Bayesian hyperparameter optimisation and nested cross-validation were employed for rigorous model tuning and validation.

Performance metrics focused on F1-score and recall, emphasising the reduction of false negatives due to their organisational consequences.  Fuzzy rule-based clustering was employed for unsupervised analysis, utilising its independence from the cluster count.  Linear integer programming was utilised for optimisation, determining objective function values under resource constraints.

To improve interpretability, explainable AI methods like SHAP waterfall plots and anchor-based "if-then" rules were utilised for comprehensive prediction analysis and actionable insights.  The integration of Gemini 1.5 Flash, a multimodal model, enabled efficient and versatile execution of repetitive tasks.  The proposed methodology exhibits a balanced strategy that integrates traditional machine learning, advanced optimisation, and explainable AI for efficient churn prediction in telecommunications.

title: Real-Time Performance Feedback and Its Impact on Human-Algorithm Interaction
affiliations: Zhejiang University, University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School, University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Operations Area, Zhejiang University and Alibaba Group

detail.title: Real-Time Performance Feedback and Its Impact on Human-Algorithm Interaction
detail.abstract: AI and digital technologies are rapidly making frontline work more algorithm-intensive. In algorithm-guided operational processes, frontline workers often retain discretion over how tasks are executed. Problem definition: In this paper, we study how making productivity and rankings continuously visible through real-time performance feedback shapes workers’ use of algorithmic recommendations, whether it reinforces adherence or encourages strategic overrides, and how these responses are reflected in operational efficiency and quality. Methodology/results: We study these questions in collaboration with Alibaba’s Cainiao logistics warehouses, where a real-time relative performance feedback system was introduced into an algorithm-guided packing process. Using package-level data and a difference-in-differences design, we find that real-time feedback improves efficiency by approximately 12%. However, the gains are not accompanied by greater algorithmic adherence. Instead, workers deviate more from the recommended box choice, using both upsizing and downsizing. These deviations are associated with substantial efficiency gains under RPF but also introduce asymmetric operational trade-offs: upsizing episodes are associated with significantly higher damage and operational-error rates, whereas the downsizing estimates are statistically insignificant. The behavioral response varies systematically with feedback signals, with different signals shaping distinct deviation strategies, and is heterogeneous across task complexity, worker experience, and system load. Managerial implications: Our findings show that real-time performance feedback changes human-algorithm interaction by shifting not only productivity but also execution strategy. In our setting, this shift manifests as increased discretionary overrides that are associated with shorter packing times but may also be related to higher operational error rates.

title: An Independent Study on Dynamic Pricing in Jakarta's Ride-Hailing Market

detail.title: An Independent Study on Dynamic Pricing in Jakarta's Ride-Hailing Market
detail.abstract: Ride-hailing platforms in Indonesia display price estimates that appear to shift constantly, and riders commonly assume these changes come from a real-time algorithm reacting to demand, rush hour, or weather. This study tests that assumption directly using three days of self-collected price data for GoRide and GrabBike across three fixed routes of varying distance in East Jakarta (72 observations in total). Prices were recorded across four sessions per day-morning, midday, afternoon, and evening-without placing any bookings. Contrary to the initial hypothesis of continuous, demand-responsive surge pricing, the data instead show a step-change pattern: prices held constant for extended stretches (in this case, roughly a day or more) before shifting once to a new level. This is clearest for Grab, whose fares across all three routes moved exactly once during the three-day window and never changed again. An apparent 137% singlesession spike on Day 1 failed to replicate on Days 2 and 3, illustrating the risk of drawing conclusions from a single anomalous observation. These findings suggest that, over short observation windows, ride-hailing fares in Jakarta behave more like periodically adjusted base fares than like minute-by-minute algorithmic surge pricing-with practical implications for how riders time their bookings and how policymakers frame algorithmic pricing practices.

title: Free to Speak, Free to Buy: Anti-SLAPP Laws and Corporate Acquisitions
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance, University of Birmingham - Birmingham Business School and University of Birmingham

detail.title: Free to Speak, Free to Buy: Anti-SLAPP Laws and Corporate Acquisitions
detail.abstract: Using the staggered enactment of anti-SLAPP laws across US states, we show that firms increase their merger and acquisition activity following these enactments. The effect is more pronounced among acquirers subject to greater financial constraints or litigation risk. Acquirers headquartered in anti-SLAPP-adopting states are also more likely to finance deals with stock and to pursue friendly deals. Investors react more positively to acquisitions announced after the passage of anti-SLAPP laws, and acquiring firms also experience better post-acquisition performance, including higher operating performance and greater innovation intensity. Overall, our results highlight the benefits of free-speech protection for corporate investment decisions.

title: The Role of Government and Technology in Ensuring Halal Integrity in Malaysia's Online Food Delivery Industry: A Conceptual Framework on the Mediating Role of Technology Adoption
affiliations: UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL, Management and Science University (MSU) and UNIVERSITY OF MAIWP INTERNATIONAL

detail.title: The Role of Government and Technology in Ensuring Halal Integrity in Malaysia's Online Food Delivery Industry: A Conceptual Framework on the Mediating Role of Technology Adoption
detail.abstract: Malaysia's online food delivery (OFD) industry has expanded rapidly over the past decade, yet this growth has introduced new points of vulnerability to the integrity of halal food as it moves from certified restaurants through gig-economy riders to the end consumer. Existing halalintegrity scholarship has largely examined regulatory, operational, and technological safeguards in isolation and within conventional, static supply chains, leaving the mechanism through which these safeguards translate into halal-integrity outcomes within the OFD environment theoretically underdeveloped. This paper addresses that gap by proposing an integrated conceptual framework in which five organizational and governance determinants halal certification standards, halal operation growth, financial credit and compliance, halal monitoring systems, and customer trust are theorized as antecedents of technology adoption, which in turn functions as the mediating mechanism linking these determinants to halal integrity in Malaysia's OFD industry. Drawing on the Technology-Organization-Environment framework, the Resource-Based View, and Institutional Theory, the paper synthesizes literature on halal governance, halal logistics, and digital traceability technologies (blockchain, the Internet of Things, and artificial intelligence) to develop eleven theoretically grounded propositions. The paper contributes a theory-integrated model that repositions technology adoption from a peripheral enabler to a central explanatory mechanism of halal integrity in digital food ecosystems, and offers regulators, OFD platform operators, and halal-certified vendors a structured basis for prioritizing digital investment. Directions for future empirical validation, including survey-based structural equation modelling, are outlined.

title: Accents and Lexis Among English Speakers in Polish IT Environments: Analyzing Its Impact on Native and Non-Native Speaker Verbal Communication

detail.title: Accents and Lexis Among English Speakers in Polish IT Environments: Analyzing Its Impact on Native and Non-Native Speaker Verbal Communication

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research study, titled “Accents and Lexis among English Speakers in Polish IT Environments: Analyzing Its Impact on Native and Non-Native Speaker Verbal Communication,” received formal ethical clearance prior to data collection. Approving Body: Mary Immaculate College / Faculty Research Ethics Committee (MIREC / JF-REC) Target Population: Adult employees in a Polish-based international IT outsourcing environment. Ethical Considerations & Protocol: Informed Consent: All participants were provided with a Information Sheet and signed an Informed Consent Form prior to participating in surveys and qualitative interviews. Anonymity & Confidentiality: All corporate names (e.g., anonymized as "XIT"), personal identifiers, and contact details were removed from interview transcripts and quantitative data sets. Voluntary Participation: Participants were informed of their right to withdraw from the study at any point without penalty or consequence to their employment status. Data Protection: Data collected was stored securely on password-protected devices in compliance with standard institutional data management guidelines.
declarations.funderStatement: self-funded

detail.abstract: This study investigates the sources of miscommunication in a Polish-based international IT outsourcing company where English serves as the lingua franca. It examines how accent variations and vocabulary choices influence communication among non-native English speakers and between non-native and native English speakers. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, this research combines quantitative data from Likert scale surveys with qualitative insights from interview transcripts to explore the impact of accents and vocabulary on communication effectiveness. The findings reveal that both accents and vocabulary choices significantly affect communication dynamics in the workplace. Accents, especially strong regional ones, are found to be a substantial barrier to understanding, particularly when they are unfamiliar. Vocabulary differences, including idiomatic expressions and industry-specific jargon, also contribute notably to misunderstandings. The study shows that job roles involving frequent communication, such as customer-facing and management positions, experience greater challenges due to these linguistic factors. Additionally, the data suggests that emotional responses, such as frustration and anxiety, are common when dealing with accent or vocabulary-related issues, influencing communication outcomes. There is a preference among participants for clear and simplified communication to minimize misunderstandings. The findings highlight the importance of role-specific language support, accent training, and intercultural competence development to improve communication effectiveness in multilingual IT environments. This research fills a gap in the existing literature by focusing on a Polish IT workplace, providing practical recommendations for enhancing communication strategies in similar settings. It underscores the need for tailored training programs to address specific communication challenges arising from accents and vocabulary differences, thereby fostering more inclusive and efficient workplaces.

title:
IPC Network 4.0 Model

An Approach to Effective Supply Chain: A Conceptual Framework and Research Agenda

detail.title:
IPC Network 4.0 Model

An Approach to Effective Supply Chain: A Conceptual Framework and Research Agenda
detail.abstract: The accuracy and the limits of ERP, WMS, and TMS architectures consistently fail when confronted with the physical findings of a modern supply chain system, especially in food, FMCG & FMCD sectors, where complexity of the Supply chain system is high and product shelf presence is the top sought factor. Latency sits at the centre of the difficulty. Digital system signals and actual shop-floor movement drift apart, whole segments of the chain go unobserved for hours at a stretch, and the systems often fail to track the mapping of a semi-finished product movement through different stages. The framework addresses the operational reality of high-velocity manufacturing: OEE stabilization, OTIF performance and shelf availability are inseparable. When one breaks, all three fail. This framework treats these elements as an interdependent system rather than isolated KPIs. Drawing on practical floor-level experience, it introduces the IPC Network Model—incorporating Industry 4.0 principles (IPC-N4.0)—to construct a highly stable, visible, and mappable supply chain management system. Unlike traditional software-first approaches, the IPC framework is grounded in physical execution. It addresses the systemic lag in traditional software (though their importance in Industry is quite high) by integrating physical Lean principles, such as dynamic Kanban implementation, with decentralized data structures like the Vendor Intelligence Index (VII) and the Product Digital Passport (PDP). The result is a pragmatic, Industry 4.0-aligned framework designed to bridge the gap between static enterprise systems and the complex, often chaotic reality of modern logistics. The framework introduces a set of new operating instruments — Inventory Health Score, Inventory Behaviour Index, Product Digital Passport, Product Journey Map, Vendor Intelligence Index, Customer Fulfilment Index, Retail Shelf Availability Index and others — together with a low-cost, blockchain-free chain-of-custody architecture suitable for FMCG cost structures. The paper illustrates the framework with publicly documented industry disruptions (KFC UK 2018, Abbott 2022, Maggi India 2015, Huy Fong Sriracha, COVID-19 FMCG disruption and others), and provides simulated but transparently constructed financial impact estimates. The paper is offered as a conceptual contribution; pilot validation in FMCG and F&B environments is explicitly recommended as the next step.

title: Green Corporate Culture

detail.title: Green Corporate Culture
detail.abstract:
Consumers encounter sustainability claims throughout their daily lives. You brush your teeth with “naturally derived” toothpaste, drink “fair trade” coffee, carry a “reusable” water bottle, and drive past advertisements for “climate-smart,” “recyclable,” and “carbon-neutral” products. Eventually, you may review a company’s sustainability report, invest in an exchange-traded fund marketed as environmentally responsible, or encounter a corporate pledge to achieve net-zero emissions. These representations shape consumer choices, investor expectation and corporate reputation. Yet a central question remains: Is sustainability part of the corporation’s DNA, or is it puffery and carefully lawyered aspiration?

This Article develops a green corporate culture authenticity test to evaluate whether voluntary sustainability commitments made by large consumer-facing companies are authentic. Authenticity matters legally because once a company voluntarily markets itself as sustainable, unsupported claims may expose it to fiduciary oversight failures, consumer-protection liability and damage corporate reputation. The Article defines “green corporate culture” as the system of oversight, incentives, information flows, controls, and verifiable metrics through which a corporation embeds sustainability priorities into its governance and operations.

To that end, this Article centers on three key factors: (1) fiduciary oversight doctrines governing “mission critical” risk, (2) disclosure controls and materiality in investor and consumer contexts, and (3) consumer fraud litigation that tests the “net impression” of sustainability narratives.  Building on this framework, this Article proposes a green corporate culture authenticity test that encompasses mission-critical oversight alignment; materiality coherence; community-impact integration; and whether a firms’ core business can plausibly support the sustainability narrative it communicates.

title:
Full-Stack Leadership without Full-Stack Sign-Off

Designing an Organisational Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance Team
affiliations: DataFakts Ltd

detail.title:
Full-Stack Leadership without Full-Stack Sign-Off

Designing an Organisational Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance Team

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Datafakts Ltd

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) governance is often allocated to whichever function first recognises the problem. In one organisation it becomes a legal project, in another a data-science standard, and in a third an ethics committee. Each approach captures part of the problem and misses the rest. AI governance is an organisational system for deciding which uses of AI are acceptable, what evidence is required, who may approve deployment, who may stop it, and how the organisation remains accountable after launch. This paper develops a practical leadership model for that system. The central proposition is that AI governance needs a full-stack lead, but never a full-stack sign-off. A hybrid lead should connect legal duties, technical facts, operational realities, business purpose and the experience of affected people. That lead should not certify the whole system alone. Legal conclusions require competent legal review. Technical claims require technical assurance. Business owners must remain accountable for purpose, benefits and residual risk. Independent audit must remain independent. People exposed to the system need a credible route to challenge outcomes and influence governance. The paper integrates the European Union (EU) Artificial Intelligence Act as amended in July 2026, United Kingdom (UK) data protection and equality law, public procurement rules, sectoral regulation, recognised standards and research from law, computer science, information systems and management. It then converts those sources into a decision architecture, role descriptions, lifecycle gates, evidence requirements, procurement controls, monitoring arrangements and an implementation programme. The result is intended as a serious operating guide rather than a collection of ethical aspirations.

title: The Price of Namelessness

detail.title: The Price of Namelessness

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests and no personal or institutional relationships that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it did not involve human participants, patients, animals, clinical intervention, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: A logo does not certify product quality, and it does not create quality. Its economic role is different: it must orient attention, secure correct brand recognition, and activate the brand equity already stored in memory. Only after that activation can past experience, advertising investment, cultural association, trust, and familiarity be converted into top-of-mind availability, choice, and willingness to pay. This article advances a stronger claim about competitive parity. When competitors reach comparable product performance, choice does not simply return to price. It returns to the logo: the fastest available sign that can capture attention, activate a brand in memory, and frame the acceptable price before detailed comparison begins. Price is downstream of that activation. A logo can therefore preserve a premium even when the functional distance between products narrows. The accumulated brand asset may remain in memory while losing its commercial effect in the moment of choice. What is reset is not the historical capital itself, but one brand's monopoly over its activation. If a competitor develops a logo with equivalent orienting power, recognition accuracy, and top-of-mind access, the contest returns to logos as decision interfaces. The paper proposes a conceptual route linking visual distinctiveness, orienting response, recognition, memory accessibility, top-of-mind status, willingness to pay, and choice. It also examines ambiguous signs that successfully capture attention but direct it toward an unintended object or category.

title: The Principle of the Awakening of Natural Leadership Original Human Singularity as the Philosophical Foundation of Natural Leadership

detail.title: The Principle of the Awakening of Natural Leadership Original Human Singularity as the Philosophical Foundation of Natural Leadership

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal, financial, or institutional interests that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical-conceptual study that did not involve human participants, patient data, personal information, or experimental procedures.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Leadership has been studied from multiple perspectives, including philosophy, sociology, psychology, management, and political science. Most of these approaches have explained the phenomenon in terms of factors such as personality, power, authority, social context, acquired competencies, or organizational relationships. By contrast, comparatively less attention has been devoted to identifying an anthropological foundation capable of explaining the emergence of natural leadership.

The present study addresses this question by formulating the Principle of the Awakening of Natural Leadership, which proposes that natural leadership emerges when the singular potentialities of each human being are discovered, developed, strengthened, and projected through a progressive process of expanding perception, thereby generating socially relevant influence that receives the free and voluntary recognition of others. This proposal builds upon the Principle of Original Human Singularity, according to which every individual constitutes a biologically, genetically, and historically unrepeatable reality from the beginning of his or her existence.

The study adopts a theoretical-conceptual approach grounded in philosophical anthropology, political philosophy, and contemporary leadership theory to develop a conceptual framework that integrates human singularity, the progressive development of perception, the strengthening of capabilities, the generation of influence, free recognition, and natural leadership. From this perspective, leadership is not conceived primarily as a condition derived from political power, institutional authority, or social position, but as a possible manifestation of human development whose legitimacy depends upon the free recognition of the community.

Finally, the study examines the implications of this proposal for understanding leadership, individual liberty, merit, and social recognition, with the aim of contributing to the contemporary debate concerning the philosophical foundations of natural leadership.

title:
From Declared Governance to Demonstrable: Governance 
Why Current AI Governance Fails Four Tests
affiliations: Swiss School of Business and Management (SSBM)

detail.title:
From Declared Governance to Demonstrable: Governance 
Why Current AI Governance Fails Four Tests

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: AI adoption has entered ordinary organisational operations faster than the governance structures built to oversee it. Stanford's 2026 AI Index reports that organisational AI adoption has reached 88 percent; Publicis Sapient's 2026 enterprise survey finds that 73 percent of AI decision-makers say AI is used regularly or across most business processes, while only 10 percent say it is core to how their business operates; PwC's 2026 AI Performance Study finds that leading companies are increasing decisions made without human intervention at 2.8 times the rate of peers; and the MIT NANDA report on enterprise generative AI found that only 5 percent of integrated pilots produced measurable financial returns. The pattern is not simply accelerating adoption. It is adoption outpacing operating transformation, oversight capacity, and decision-level evidence. This working paper asks what the reality of AI governance looks like under those conditions. It argues that current AI governance struggles to pass four operational tests: accountability, auditability, scale, and durability. Drawing on public policy materials, corporate and institutional surveys, selected peer-reviewed research, incidentmonitoring literature, and the Australian Robodebt case, the paper distinguishes declared governance-policies, principles, checklists, vendor assurances, and retrospective compliance artefacts-from demonstrable governance: evidence that can show when a consequential decision was made, why it was made, by whom it was authorised or reviewed, which affected stakeholders and consequences were considered, and whether the outcome remained aligned with the purpose for which the system was deployed. The Robodebt case, although not an AI case, shows why the gap is architectural rather than merely technological. If a deterministic and technically explainable system can operate unlawfully for years at national scale despite repeated warnings, then explainability alone cannot provide governance. The systems have changed, but the burden of decision-making, accountability, and consequence has not.

title:
Capital in Motion 
Global Equity Allocation and the M&A Cycle at Mid-Year 2026: Who Is Investing, Where the Money Is Moving, and What Comes Next
affiliations: Szymon Zephan Capital (SZC Group)

detail.title:
Capital in Motion 
Global Equity Allocation and the M&A Cycle at Mid-Year 2026: Who Is Investing, Where the Money Is Moving, and What Comes Next

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Managing Partner at SZC Group
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: SZC Group

detail.abstract: This paper maps the ownership, allocation and transaction pathways of global equity capital through the second quarter of 2026. It distinguishes institutional investors, pension and sovereign funds, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds, private equity and venture capital, family offices, retail investors, high-net-worth individuals and ultra-high-net-worth individuals. For each group, the analysis separates assets from current flows, investor domicile from target geography, and public equities from private transactions, IPOs and mergers and acquisitions. The evidence covers North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America, the Middle East and Africa and integrates market performance, capital formation, transaction value, deal count, sector allocation, financing conditions and regulatory risk. The central finding is that capital markets recovered in value faster than in breadth. Global equities advanced and IPO and M&A proceeds strengthened, but a small number of very large issuers and transactions accounted for a disproportionate share of the improvement. Artificial intelligence, power systems, advanced manufacturing, infrastructure, defence and healthcare attracted strategic capital, while ordinary sponsor exits and mid-market access remained less reliable. Four probability-weighted scenarios assess the remainder of 2026. The base case is selective broadening rather than indiscriminate risk-taking. The paper recommends that investors and policymakers measure ex-megadeal value, median transaction access, realized exits, regulatory completion and regional and sector breadth alongside headline totals.

title: "Incentives" Under the Real Plan: The Behavioral Economic Foundation of the URV Choice Architecture, the Brazilian Anti-Inflation Nudge
affiliations: University Federal Fluminense

detail.title: "Incentives" Under the Real Plan: The Behavioral Economic Foundation of the URV Choice Architecture, the Brazilian Anti-Inflation Nudge
detail.abstract: This study explores the innovative application of behavioral economics principles in the Real Plan, implemented in 1994. By anchoring prices to the Unidade Real de Valor (URV), which was indexed to the US dollar, the plan aimed to mitigate the effects of hyperinflation and establish a stable reference for prices. The work seeks to define what this reference would be and how it is formed through the literature on reference-dependent preference theory in the context of prices. The generalization of the value function first proposed by Kahneman and Tversky in their prospect theory will be used, as Thaler concept of transaction and acquisition utility. Finally, the similarities between the implementation process of the URV and the Nudge theory will be observed.

title: The Purpose of Money: Exploring Generation Z's Perceptions of Wealth, Success, and Financial Fulfillment: A Qualitative Study of Generation Z Young Adults

detail.title: The Purpose of Money: Exploring Generation Z's Perceptions of Wealth, Success, and Financial Fulfillment: A Qualitative Study of Generation Z Young Adults
detail.abstract: Money has long been recognized as a multidimensional construct that extends beyond its economic function to influence personal identity, social status, psychological well-being, and life satisfaction. For Generation Z, a cohort shaped by rapid technological advancement, digital finance, economic uncertainty, and pervasive social media influence, perceptions of money are increasingly complex and value-driven. This study explores how Generation Z young adults perceive the purpose of money, wealth, success, and financial fulfillment through a qualitative phenomenological approach. The study seeks to understand the meanings young adults attach to financial resources, the factors influencing their financial aspirations, and the relationship between financial achievement and personal fulfillment. Data are conceptually based on semi-structured, in-depth interviews analyzed using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis framework to identify recurring patterns and shared lived experiences. The findings suggest that Generation Z perceives money as a means of achieving autonomy, security, opportunity, and personal freedom rather than merely accumulating wealth. Financial success is viewed as a balance between economic stability, meaningful work, mental well-being, and the ability to pursue individual goals. Participants also emphasize the significant roles of family financial socialization, financial literacy, entrepreneurial aspirations, digital financial technologies, and social media in shaping financial attitudes and behaviors. The study contributes to the growing literature on youth financial behavior by proposing a more holistic understanding of financial fulfillment that integrates economic, psychological, and social dimensions. The findings offer practical implications for educators, policymakers, financial institutions, employers, and career development professionals seeking to improve financial well-being among Generation Z.

title: Case Study: The Fredericksburg Ring — Five Jurisdictions, One Corridor, and the I-95 Path South
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Case Study: The Fredericksburg Ring — Five Jurisdictions, One Corridor, and the I-95 Path South
detail.abstract: Since 2022, the five jurisdictions surrounding the Rappahannock River fall line (Spotsylvania, Stafford, Caroline, and King George counties, and the independent City of Fredericksburg) have approved data center campuses totaling at least 5.4 gigawatts of reported capacity and roughly 44 million square feet of entitled building area. No regional body has added those numbers up. This case study does. The Fredericksburg ring is where the Northern Virginia diffusion wave crosses the river. Every project priced out of Loudoun or blocked in Prince William and moving south on I-95 passes through these five governments first, and since at least 2018 the five have held themselves to an identical $1.25 per $100 tax rate on data center equipment, a regional compact built to keep any one of them from being shopped against the others. The compact held. Everything else diverged. Spotsylvania approved more than sixteen million square feet, watched an election turn on the issue, and in February 2026 imposed a moratorium on any new data center. Stafford defended by-right approval in March 2025, then adopted Virginia's most stringent setback that October and grandfathered all five of its approved campuses six weeks later. Caroline invented a new zoning district to receive Amazon, took a 900-megawatt campus by right at a former flea market, and is defending its Rappahannock withdrawal permit against the Rappahannock Tribe in circuit court. King George approved a $6 billion coal-plant-to-data-center conversion, un-approved it after one election, and meets Amazon at trial in September 2026. The City of Fredericksburg, fiscally cornered and seven votes unanimous, built a by-right overlay district for a $10 billion campus that has yet to break ground. Five governments, one demand wave, one shared river, five different instruments. The corridor is the closest thing the series has to a natural experiment in institutional behavior, and its developers treat it as a single market: Amazon appears in four of the five jurisdictions, STACK Infrastructure in three, AVAIO in one county three times. The report documents the approval chronologies, the instruments, the rate postures, the water ledger, and the cumulative arithmetic nobody totals, and flags two jurisdictions, Spotsylvania and Stafford, whose records are now deep enough to warrant standalone treatment in future versions of this series.

title: Too Motivating to Be Believed: Communication and the Production of Evidence

detail.title: Too Motivating to Be Believed: Communication and the Production of Evidence
detail.abstract: I study communication across successive decision makers when effort determines not only payoffs but whether informative evidence exists at all. Each agent privately observes an effort cost, takes an unobserved action, sees a public outcome, and sends a cheap-talk causal assessment to her successor. The sender values her successor's success and underweights her successor's effort cost. Under moderate motivational bias, every equilibrium surviving an action-changing-neologism test separates pessimistic and optimistic sender types and learns the state. Under stronger bias, all types prefer effort, so after a causally confounded failure no message can induce experimentation in any equilibrium. Inactivity then makes outcomes uninformative and a false no-experimentation state becomes absorbing. Stronger motivation can therefore make learning worse. Outcome-contingent verification repairs the mechanism sharply: auditing every failure and no success uniquely minimizes discounted audit cost among stationary rules that guarantee learning in every equilibrium, while any failure-audit rate below one leaves a positive probability of permanent shutdown. An explicit conditional-adoption cutoff determines when targeted verification is worth its cost; for an open interval of costs it is desirable even though blanket effort certification is not.

title: The River-to-Recreation Conversion Framework: A Middle-Range Theory of Value Translation and Sustainable Urban Infrastructure Finance

detail.title: The River-to-Recreation Conversion Framework: A Middle-Range Theory of Value Translation and Sustainable Urban Infrastructure Finance
detail.abstract: Contingent valuation and stated preference studies have produced robust evidence that households value environmental restoration. What remains largely unexplained is why that documented value so frequently fails to become durable maintenance funding. This paper introduces the River-to-Recreation Conversion Framework, built around a single analytical distinction: value formation (V)—the perception of benefit from a restored ecosystem—operates through a different institutional logic than value translation (η)—the conversion of that perceived benefit into recurring financial commitments. Value translation efficiency is a property of the institutional channel connecting recognized environmental value to realized maintenance finance, not reducible to trust, income, compliance, or general institutional quality. The paper specifies conditions under which the central claims would be falsified. Extensions include an institutional learning feedback loop, a Cultural-Symbolic Disamenity Mechanism, a financing-logic typology, the Capital Completion Paradox, and a portfolio optimization logic. Six cities are examined as illustrative applications. The paper closes with actionable policy imperatives and an empirical research agenda.

title: Increasing public spending in the care economy: a dynamic modelling assessment of the socio-economic and environmental implications for Italy
affiliations: Instituto Superior Tecnico, University of Pisa and Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária (INIAV, I.P.) - MARETEC

detail.title: Increasing public spending in the care economy: a dynamic modelling assessment of the socio-economic and environmental implications for Italy
detail.abstract: Health, long-term care, childcare and education services are essential for human flourishing within planetary boundaries. Feminist macroeconomics indicates that expanding formal care sectors not only enhances well-being but also raises employment and output while reducing gender disparities. Yet quantitative assessments through dynamic macroeconomic models remain scarce and the environmental consequences underexplored, leaving the overall socio-economic and environmental implications of expanding public care services unclear. Here, we use the ecological macroeconomic simulation model Eurogreen+ calibrated to Italy to address this gap. The model features an input-output structure with sector-specific endogenous innovation, a labour market segmented by skill and gender, and multiple energy carriers and electricity-generation technologies. We compare a baseline scenario that maintains current care provision with an ambitious scenario aligning it with best-performing countries, also accounting for the labour productivity spillovers this expansion may trigger. We find that expanding public care services raises output with a long-run fiscal multiplier above 1.6, and that over half of the additional spending self-finances through increased tax revenues. The debt-to-GDP ratio nonetheless rises in the long run, emissions increase, and gender and income inequality remain broadly unaltered. With no productivity spillovers, each new care job generates an additional job in other sectors. However, with productivity spillovers job losses in other sectors outweigh care job creation – despite faster GDP growth (that further raises emissions). These findings reveal potential unintended socio-economic and environmental consequences of expanding care services, highlighting the need for carefully designed complementary policies.

title: Modeling Experience Effects from Related but Non-Identical ChoiceContexts
affiliations: , Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: Modeling Experience Effects from Related but Non-Identical ChoiceContexts
detail.abstract: A large strand of the choice modeling literature has examined how priorexperience affects subsequent choices in repeated-choice settings, where ex-perience is often represented as persistence toward previously chosen alter-natives. However, many real-world choices are cross-contextual. Decisionmakers face a choice context that is new in its exact form while drawing onprior experiences from related, but non-identical, contexts. In such settings,prior experience may not only create alternative-specific persistence, but alsoinform how observable attributes are interpreted and weighted in the currentchoice context.To address this gap, this paper develops a constructed-state approachfor incorporating fragmented cross-contextual histories into current choicemodels. The approach converts prior encounters into two decision-relevantstates: a patient-level general experience state, which allows prior experi-ence to moderate attribute valuation, and an alternative-specific momentumstate, which captures persistence toward previously experienced alternatives.We apply the framework to hospital choice among South Korean patients un-dergoing first-time total knee arthroplasty using National Health Insuranceclaims data. The constructed-history specification better explains patients’observed choices, demonstrating that constructed experience states providea systematic way to extend choice models to settings in which prior historiesare fragmented across related but non-identical contexts.

title: Social Polarization in Response to Contagion
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Social Polarization in Response to Contagion
detail.abstract: Abstract I examine how the risk of contagion affects activity levels in a model of endogenous network formation. Whether a disease outbreak dies out early or expands into a full-blown epidemic depends on the variation between individuals in how likely they are to spread the disease to others. In a behavioral model in which people choose the level of contact they have with others in response to news of disease outbreak, highly connected people respond differently from people with few social connections. When risk is high, highly social people can become fatalistic, and increase their social activity. Endogenous choice can reverse the impact of activity dispersion on the final size of an outbreak.

title: Integrated Assessment Modeling of Water and the Economy: A CGE Application to Insurance Mechanisms under Hydrological Anomalies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of São Paulo (USP), University of São Paulo (USP), University of São Paulo (USP) and University of Sao Paulo (USP) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Integrated Assessment Modeling of Water and the Economy: A CGE Application to Insurance Mechanisms under Hydrological Anomalies
detail.abstract: This study proposes an Integrated Assessment Modeling (IAM) framework to estimate the direct, indirect, regional, and interregional economic impacts of climate-induced hydrological anomalies on Brazilian agriculture and to assess their implications for climate-risk insurance pricing. The framework integrates econometric estimates of crop sensitivity to precipitation and temperature anomalies, climate projections from Phase 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP), SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, an interregional Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model representing Brazil’s 12 Hydrographic Regions (B-MARIA-12HR), and the Hydrological Risk Transfer Model (MTRH-SHS). The analysis projects climate-related productivity shocks for the period 2015-2100 and evaluates their propagation through interregional production networks and supply chains. Results indicate that rising temperatures and unstable precipitation patterns generate heterogeneous but predominantly negative impacts on agricultural productivity, Gross Regional Product (GRP), and national economic activity, with stronger effects under SSP5-8.5. The most vulnerable regions include Paraguay, Parnaíba, Amazon, and Tocantins-Araguaia hydrographic regions. The estimated present value of cumulative Gross Domestic Product (GDP) losses reaches approximately BRL 2.6 billion under SSP2-4.5 and BRL 4.1 billion under SSP5-8.5 per year. By integrating CGE outputs into the insurance framework, the study estimates actuarially fair premiums that substantially exceed current Brazilian rural insurance premiums, suggesting that existing mechanisms may underestimate long-term systemic climate risks. The findings highlight the importance of incorporating indirect and interregional economic effects into climate adaptation finance and agricultural insurance design.

title: Bubbles and Ponzi Finance
affiliations: Chess Ed and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Bubbles and Ponzi Finance
detail.abstract: We give a unified account of speculative bubbles and Ponzi finance. The theory is the trading option of Harrison and Kreps (1978): with heterogeneous priors and a short sale constraint the price exceeds every investor's own valuation, and the excess is the right to sell to someone else. The same fixed point prices fiat money, a chartered monopoly and a reflexive token. Two quantities organise everything. The trading option Γ = p-F measures how much of a price is the right to trade rather than to hold. The funding ratio θ measures what share of payouts to exiting claimants is met from revenue earned outside the set of claimants. They are orthogonal, and together they place bubbles, fiat money, subsidised yields and outright fraud on one map. The funding ratio drives the dynamics: liabilities compound at (1-θ)r, lifetime is bounded by log N/ log(1 + (1-θ)r), and honest finance and fraud become endpoints of a continuum. A bubble is a price with an equivalent local martingale measure that is strict; a Ponzi promise admits no measure at all, being an advertised arbitrage rather than an overvalued security. Three results follow. The trading option has an exact compensator representation, the discrete time shadow of the strict local martingale property, bounded by disagreement times patience. Reflexivity splits the valuation fixed point into a stable and an unstable root and destroys it past a threshold. In floating price convertibles the holder is long a floor rather than a call, so vega is negative and linear reflexivity extinguishes the equity in finite time. Empirically, across twelve schemes from 1879 to 2022, lifetime and principal at risk both fall in the promised rate, with rank correlations of-0.77 and-0.73 and a fitted duration elasticity of 0.64 against a theoretical frontier of unity. Expected loss is maximised by modest promises, which inverts the folk heuristic. We also give a detection statistic using only the sign of each reported return: on the Fairfield Sentry record the frequency of losing months implies an annual Sharpe of 4.89 against the 0.656 the stated strategy could deliver. Charles Ponzi is the canonical case of a real arbitrage with a hard capacity bound, and OneCoin the opposite limit. We cover the experiments of Smith, Suchanek and Williams (1988); four centuries of cases from the Dutch East India Company through 1720, Poyais, the railway manias and the 1929 investment trusts; the stone money of Yap as reported by Friedman (1992); gold and fiat following Bernstein (2000); the Hyperliquid buyback; and the demography of trading options, where Durand (1957), Eatwell (2004) and Boulding (1965) meet.

title: How Does Market Fragmentation Affect Price Dynamics? Evidence From an Agent-Based Model
affiliations: University of Vermont - College of Engineering and Mathematics, MITRE Corporation, MITRE Corporation and The MITRE Corporation

detail.title: How Does Market Fragmentation Affect Price Dynamics? Evidence From an Agent-Based Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: C.M.V.O., M.T.T.K., and B.F.T. were supported by MITRE’s Financial Innovation Lab. E.R.C. was supported by the MITRE PhD Fellowship in Computational Finance within the Vermont Complex Systems Institute at the University of Vermont.

detail.abstract: The U.S. equity market is fragmented and has become more so over recent decades. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has warned that increased fragmentation could decrease price competition among orders, in turn impairing price discovery and creating excessive shortterm volatility. However, financial agent-based models (ABMs) still largely represent trading as consolidated, limiting their application for studying how current market structure may shape aggregate behavior. In this study, we extend an existing fragmented-market ABM by adding trading strategies adapted from prior work, using the resulting model to compare price dynamics generated under consolidated and fragmented configurations. We find that the interaction between market structure and the information acted on by agents is central to how fragmentation affects price formation and aggregate returns. When agents act only on price quotes from their local exchange, market fragmentation can amplify extreme price moves and concentrate them in time. The resulting returns exhibit heavier tails, stronger volatility clustering, and less persistent linear autocorrelation than the consolidatedmarket benchmark. When agents instead act based on cross-market price quotes from a consolidated feed, the effects of fragmentation on the generated price dynamics are much smaller, though latency on that feed makes them more visible. Adding a latency arbitrageur to the fragmented configurations has minimal incremental effect. More broadly, the study illustrates how ABMs with explicit market microstructure can be used to compare structural scenarios and clarify the mechanisms linking market organization to aggregate behavior.

title: Deep Disposals, Deeper Concerns: Investigating Public Opposition to Submarine Tailings in Arctic Norway
affiliations: Centre for Applied Research at NHH and University of Warsaw

detail.title: Deep Disposals, Deeper Concerns: Investigating Public Opposition to Submarine Tailings in Arctic Norway
detail.abstract: The green transition is increasing demand for metals and minerals, and Norway has several deposits of these resources. At the same time, the use of submarine tailings disposal (STD) in fjords and coastal waters has generated substantial public opposition to new mining projects. We report results from a survey of residents in Finnmark county, where the mine is located, other Arctic counties, and Oslo, the capital area. The survey included a discrete choice experiment in which respondents chose between the approved mining plan and alternatives with stricter environmental regulation, lower environmental impacts, fewer local jobs, and a household cost. Respondents displayed substantial willingness to pay to avoid the current plan and to reduce environmental damage. Contrary to a conventional not-in-my-backyard pattern, residents closer to the proposed mine were more likely to choose the current plan. However, their marginal willingness to pay for seabed recovery, salmon protection, jobs, and cost did not differ systematically from that of other respondents. Hybrid mixed logit results show that general acceptance of STD and policy orientation explain more preference heterogeneity than information about the specific project. These findings suggest that policy responses should address broad concerns about STD technology as well as the distribution of local benefits and environmental risks.

title: Driving on Unequal Exchange: Imperial Labour Transfers in the Global Automobile System and the True Speed of Car

detail.title: Driving on Unequal Exchange: Imperial Labour Transfers in the Global Automobile System and the True Speed of Car
detail.abstract: This paper revisits Ivan Illich’s concept of ”effective speed” by incorporating the global redistribution of embodied labour that sustains automobile systems. While existing estimates measure the time motorists must work to afford car use, they omit the labour performed abroad and transferred through ecological unequal exchange., We extend this framework by introducing an additional time component: the net embodied labour imported through global supply chains. Using multi-regional input–output analysis (EXIOBASE) combined with material flow data, we compute a corrected effective speed for 31 countries and disaggregate results by income decile., We show that automobile effective speed is partly the result of assymetric transfers. High-income countries gain up to 5 km/h through unequal exchange, while lower-income countries experience corresponding losses. The global median effective speed is approximately 15 km/h: for half of the world’s motorists, the car does not outperform the bicycle., However, at the national level, we identify a mechanism of ”imperial overcompensation”: in net-importing countries, unequal exchange raises the effective speed of lower and middle income groups above what domestic redistribution alone would allow, and, absent this transfer, the car would fail to beat the bicycle well into the middle-income deciles of wealthy countries., These findings suggest that technological efficiency is a relational property of the world economy and that resistance to transport decarbonisation could reflect material interests structured by global labour transfers.

title: Allocative Governance under Constraint: Validated Allocative Events, Binding Admissibility, and Contestability in Reinforcing Digital Systems

detail.title: Allocative Governance under Constraint: Validated Allocative Events, Binding Admissibility, and Contestability in Reinforcing Digital Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual paper does not involve human participants, patients, or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly allocate value through events: creator payouts, referral rewards, API settlement, and platform-mediated labor compensation. These systems are often framed as problems of pricing, attribution, or fraud detection. This paper argues that they should instead be understood as problems of allocative governance under constraint: deciding which observed activities may become legitimate units of value allocation when behavior adapts to reward surfaces, validation capacity is limited, and access to recourse is uneven. The central contribution is the concept of the validated allocative event: an observed event that must be measurable, admissible for value allocation, and mappable to settlement. The concept extends earlier work on event-level monetization by moving from payout design toward broader questions of distribution, contestability, and institutional recourse. Building on a reinforcement-under-constraint perspective, the paper treats allocation as a reinforcing system in which initiation expands activity, reinforcement amplifies reward-seeking behavior, and selection determines which candidate events may count. The paper develops a conceptual and diagnostic governance interface for contested digital allocation rather than a new estimator, formal mechanism, or empirical test. It links validated allocative events with binding admissibility, auditability, replayability, contestability, and versioned rule commitments. To make the interface operationally inspectable, the paper outlines diagnostic measures and evaluation protocols for selection latency, audit completeness, false exclusion, dispute resolvability, and motion-value drift. The broader claim is that reinforcing digital systems do not remain fair or governable by measuring more activity; they require explicit allocative selection under constraint, especially where access to reward and recourse is unevenly distributed.

title: Systems of production with energy as an interface with nature: a note on reproducibility and viability
affiliations: The University of Western Australia

detail.title: Systems of production with energy as an interface with nature: a note on reproducibility and viability
detail.abstract: The purpose of this note is to provide a structural interpretation of the economic consequences of energy availability without requiring a bio-physical reformulation of production theory. It treats energy as an input from nature to a Leontief production system. This has two distinct consequences. First, it determines the minimum output vector required for system reproducibility. Second, it determines the system's distance from a viability threshold. This helps explain why energy seems to play a limited role in some empirical analysis despite being fundamental. It also has implications for understanding the relation between energy and economic growth.

title:
Intelligent Audit Systems: Development of Advanced Financial Ratios and AI-Based Audit Methodology 
Integrating Financial Statements, ERP Systems, and Cash Flow Analysis

detail.title:
Intelligent Audit Systems: Development of Advanced Financial Ratios and AI-Based Audit Methodology 
Integrating Financial Statements, ERP Systems, and Cash Flow Analysis
detail.abstract: Contemporary audit practice, anchored in ISA 520 analytical procedures, relies predominantly on aggregated financial ratios computed from historical balance-sheet data. This paradigm exhibits fundamental limitations in environments characterized by complex enterprise resource planning (ERP) ecosystems, high-volume transaction flows, and sophisticated manipulation schemes. The present paper proposes the Audit Intelligent System (AIS)a four-layer methodological architecture that integrates financial-statement analytics, ERP operational data, behavioral pattern recognition, and artificialintelligence-driven anomaly detection. We introduce and formally define six advanced audit ratios-RCRT, RTBC, IDC, RFE, RPC, and RCTeach targeting specific risk dimensions that remain undetected by conventional ratio analysis. A composite Risk Score model is formalized, assigning differential weights to each analytical layer. The methodology is benchmarked against the ISA 520 standard, demonstrating superior coverage across transaction granularity, cash-flow alignment, and realtime risk detection. Implications for professional audit standards, regulatory frameworks, and future empirical research are discussed.

title: State Capacity and Fiscal Exposure in the Late Ottoman Empire: The Ex-Post Budgets of the Irād-ı Cedīd Treasury, 1793-1807
affiliations: Osmaniye Korkut Ata University

detail.title: State Capacity and Fiscal Exposure in the Late Ottoman Empire: The Ex-Post Budgets of the Irād-ı Cedīd Treasury, 1793-1807
detail.abstract: Between 1793 and 1807, the Ottoman Empire financed its centralized, standing infantry, through a newly created treasury, the Irād-ı Cedīd, funded by centralizing existing tax farms and life-annuity revenue instruments under direct treasury control, not through new taxation. This paper presents the complete ex-post budget series of this treasury across all fourteen fiscal years of its operation, drawing on the Ottoman archival account books. The series shows a clear asymmetry between the treasury’s two sides. On the revenue side, centralized traditional revenues rose unevenly from roughly 45 percent of total income to a peak of 61 percent. On the expenditure side, extraordinary military outlays driven by external security threats exceeded half of total spending in the peak crisis year and pushed the treasury into recorded deficit in three of its fourteen years, concentrated in 1797-99 and 1801. This asymmetry is largely absent from the treasury’s founding charter and from existing qualitative accounts of the reform. The findings indicate that fiscal centralization and fiscal exposure are separable dimensions of early modern state capacity, since an administration could consolidate revenue collection while remaining structurally exposed to the spending side. Because revenue centralization is often treated as the principal empirical marker of state capacity in the fiscal-military state literature, this case suggests that such measures capture administrative reach without capturing budgetary sustainability. The Irād-ı Cedīd case extends this literature beyond its predominantly European empirical base, using a complete, year-by-year account of realized fiscal performance.

title: Longitudinal Evidence for the Effects of Hurricane Experience on Adaptation vs. Mitigation Behaviors and Policy Preferences
affiliations: Princeton University, University of Groningen and Princeton University

detail.title: Longitudinal Evidence for the Effects of Hurricane Experience on Adaptation vs. Mitigation Behaviors and Policy Preferences
detail.abstract: Extreme weather events are increasing in frequency and severity due to climate change. Prior research finds that exposure to such events can shift climate concern and policy preferences. Some scholars speculate that growing direct experiences with the impacts of climate change might thus catalyze climate concern, action, and policy support, including among groups that tend to oppose climate action. Yet, evidence for the impact of extreme weather events on climate-related attitudes and behaviors is mixed, typically based on cross-sectional data and thus correlational, and has tended to focus on risk perceptions. We know little about how exposure to extreme weather shapes individual preferences for different policies or behaviors—such as those focused on mitigation or adaptation. Leveraging an original longitudinal panel dataset collected before and after the U.S. hurricane season, we assess the relationship between experience and preferences for adaptation vs. mitigation. We find that recent hurricane experience has nuanced effects that vary with the outcome variable, experience severity and party affiliation. While recent hurricane experience can increase mitigation and adaptation intentions among those who experience significant harms, it can also reduce adaptation intentions among those with mild experience. These findings are consistent with an informational account, whereby experience provides a signal about one’s own vulnerability and need for adaptive action. Critically, longitudinal results differ substantially from cross-sectional results, which show a strong positive and significant association between experience and climate worry, behavior and policy preferences. Our findings show the potential for extreme weather experience to reduce adaptation behaviors.

title:
Decision Risk Pattern Intelligence (DRPI) A Longitudinal Governance Documentation Standard for AI-Supported Justice Environments 
Conceptual Foundations, Scope, and Implications for AI Governance
affiliations: Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis and Indiana University, Indianapolis - Indiana University Indianapolis

detail.title:
Decision Risk Pattern Intelligence (DRPI) A Longitudinal Governance Documentation Standard for AI-Supported Justice Environments 
Conceptual Foundations, Scope, and Implications for AI Governance
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports institutional decision-making across corrections, courts, community supervision, law enforcement, and other justice-sector organizations. Contemporary AI governance has substantially advanced responsible deployment through frameworks emphasizing transparency, accountability, lifecycle risk management, technical assurance, documentation, and meaningful human oversight. While organizations increasingly document operational conditions before deployment and reconstruct governance environments following significant events, comparatively less attention has been devoted to documenting recurring governance conditions that emerge across operational decision-making over time. This paper introduces Decision Risk Pattern Intelligence (DRPI) as the longitudinal governance documentation standard within the broader conceptual architecture of Justice Decision Observability (JDO). Rather than functioning as predictive analytics, statistical modeling, organizational performance evaluation, or algorithmic risk assessment, DRPI documents recurring operational decision environments observed across multiple institutional decisions. The objective is to improve institutional understanding of persistent governance conditions capable of informing organizational learning, governance maturity, institutional continuity, transparency, and responsible AI governance. The paper argues that recurring governance conditions constitute legitimate objects of governance documentation independent of technical system evaluation, compliance assessment, or post-event investigation. By establishing longitudinal governance documentation as a complementary governance perspective alongside prospective and retrospective governance documentation, Decision Risk Pattern Intelligence expands the temporal architecture of Justice Decision Observability while deliberately avoiding discussion of proprietary implementation methodologies, analytical procedures, documentation instruments, or governance protocols.

title: The Ghost in the Mosh Pit: A Dialectical Inquiry into the Punk Ontology of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: The Ghost in the Mosh Pit: A Dialectical Inquiry into the Punk Ontology of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has triggered significant cultural anxiety, notably within counter-cultural spaces such as the punk scene in Estonia. Drawing parallels to historical neo-Luddite reactions against the steam engine, synthesizers, and the internet, this paper philosophically examines whether generative AI models fundamentally align with or oppose the "punk" ethos. By utilizing a dialectical approach, we analyze AI as a tool of corporate hegemony (the Establishment) versus open-source AI as a decentralized, copyright-destroying tool of digital DIY (the Underground). Ultimately, we propose a framework to evaluate the ontological status of AI within subcultural theory, aiming to move the discourse beyond mistargeted tech-phobia toward structural critique.

reference: Markets: Perspectives from Economic and Social Theory, W.A. Jackson, London: Routledge, 2019, pp. 3-11
title: Defining Markets
affiliations: University of York - Department of Economics and Related Studies

detail.title: Defining Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: Markets: Perspectives from Economic and Social Theory, W.A. Jackson, London: Routledge, 2019, pp. 3-11

detail.abstract: Markets have never had a single agreed definition, despite their prominence in the economic literature. Casual use of the word 'market' allows it to be conflated with broader notions of exchange and leads to inconsistencies. This chapter ponders the difficulties surrounding a market definition and asks how they might be overcome. Markets are first placed within the context of the whole economy, as a subset of distribution and exchange. Various possible characteristics of a market are considered, along with the case for strong and weak definitions and for a scale of 'marketness' that avoids any market/non-market boundary. Discussion then moves on to look at whether we should have a theoretical concept of the ideal market, given the diversity of actual trading. The chapter ends with an outline of the aims and structure of the book.

title: Road-User Acceptance of External Human-Machine Interfaces for Autonomous Vehicles: Evidence from Virtual Reality Experiments with Drivers, Cyclists, and Pedestrians
affiliations: University of New Mexico, University of Westminster, University of New Mexico, Rowan University, Texas State University and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Road-User Acceptance of External Human-Machine Interfaces for Autonomous Vehicles: Evidence from Virtual Reality Experiments with Drivers, Cyclists, and Pedestrians
detail.abstract: Effective communication between autonomous vehicles (AVs) and other road users is essential for safe interactions in mixed-traffic environments. External human-machine interfaces (eHMIs) can communicate vehicle intent, reduce uncertainty, and support understanding among pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers. This study examines road users' acceptance of eHMI designs through a virtual reality experiment involving simulated interactions with an AV. In total, 310 interaction trials were analysed across pedestrian, cyclist, and driver scenarios. The concepts included text displays, windshield light bands, side-mirror arrows, side-mounted displays, and a baseline without an eHMI. After each interaction, participants reported perceived trust, perceived risk, mental and physical workload, and acceptance. Trust emerged as a central factor supporting eHMI acceptance, whereas perceived risk and mental demand reduced willingness to accept these systems. Cyclists showed the highest acceptance while also reporting relatively high perceived risk, reflecting their greater vulnerability in AV interactions. Pedestrians exhibited moderate trust and greater sensitivity to cognitive workload, highlighting the need for clear and intuitive communication requiring minimal effort. Drivers reported relatively low workload and appeared more familiar with vehicle-based cues, although their acceptance still depended on clear and reliable communication of AV intent. Age-related differences further emphasised the importance of simple, accessible, and understandable designs. Overall, effective eHMIs should communicate vehicle intention clearly, remain visible, align with vehicle movement, and address the differing needs of road-user groups. These findings provide practical guidance for inclusive AV communication systems that strengthen trust, reduce uncertainty, and support safety in future urban mobility.

title: ROOT: A Framework for Closing the Data-Decision Gap in Complex Organizations

detail.title: ROOT: A Framework for Closing the Data-Decision Gap in Complex Organizations

The framework and illustrative cases presented in this paper draw on the author's professional experience, including experience gained at these organizations. This paper was not commissioned, reviewed, or funded by either organization, and does not represent their official positions.

The illustrative cases described (Section 8) are drawn from professional practice experience and are presented in aggregated, non-identifying form with respect to individuals; no IRB or ethics committee review was required or sought.
