The planned data collection is fully anonymous by design: no name, e-mail address, or identifier is collected at any point, and participants are informed at collection that anonymized, aggregated results may be used in research publications. The measurement battery presents hypothetical decision scenarios and is administered within institutional professional development programs and, prospectively, through online recruitment of general-population samples under the same anonymous architecture.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The research was supported by Pensata, Inc.

detail.abstract: Traditional credit scoring, notably FICO, penalizes the volatile cash flows typical of entrepreneurs and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). We propose the BYLAS Score, which treats prospect-theoretic biases not as risks but as stable, measurable features of the borrower. Embedding risk sensitivity (α), loss aversion (λ), and probability weighting (γ) in a continuous-time cash-flow model yields a closed-form map from biased projections to objective firm fundamentals (μ, σ), which in the baseline regime reduces to a single γ-dependent adjustment to the stated drift. The instrument—which measures each subject twice within a single sitting, under a normal frame and an induced-stress frame—the identification strategy, and the hypotheses are pre-specified in advance of data collection. The central prediction is that subjects near-identical on observable attributes nonetheless separate into distinct behavioral archetypes, with those attributes explaining only a small share of the behavioral variance. We draw out the implications for credit-thin and low-FICO populations, proposing tailored revenue-based financing, micro-credit, and ESG guardrails.

title: The History of Establishing the Asean Intergovernmental Commission on Human Rights: The External World and Internal Regional Dynamics
affiliations: Mahidol University International College

detail.title: The History of Establishing the Asean Intergovernmental Commission on Human Rights: The External World and Internal Regional Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper examines the historical establishment of the ASEAN Intergovernmental Commission on Human Rights (AICHR) by analyzing the convergence of external pressures and internal regional dynamics. It identifies three primary macro-level drivers: the influence of the Western unipolar moment following the Cold War, the search for international credibility and relevance, and the domestic processes of democratization within key Southeast Asian states. The establishment of AICHR also served as a strategic response to the sensitivities of post-colonial statehood and the preservation of state sovereignty. By creating its own regional mechanism, ASEAN sought to emulate the institutional paradigms of the European Union, the African Union, and the Organization of American States, thereby signaling its legitimacy to the international community. Crucially, AICHR was conceived as a 'buffer' against external interference, allowing regional elites to control the human rights narrative and protect themselves from the perceived threats of 'unwanted globalization' or foreign policy tools used by Western partners to infringe on domestic affairs. This statist approach prioritizes a state-based security view of human rights over a society-or individual-based perspective, framing human rights as a component of national development and capacity building.

title: State Ownership and Deposit Safety
affiliations: Imperial College Business School

detail.title: State Ownership and Deposit Safety
detail.abstract: Do depositors see state-owned banks as safer? The isolated, unexpected failure of Banco Santos, a private bank, in November 2004 raised the perceived risk of uninsured deposits in Brazil. Time deposits at state-owned banks grew 6.4 log points per month faster than at private banks, 45 log points over seven months. Excluding the largest banks leaves the estimate unchanged, separating ownership from too-big-to-fail size. Demand and savings deposits, whose clients were almost all fully insured, show no movement.

title: Farms Typologies and Their Impact on the Development of Rural Areas in Moldova
affiliations: State Agrarian University of Moldova, Students and Academy of Economic Studies of Moldova

detail.title: Farms Typologies and Their Impact on the Development of Rural Areas in Moldova
detail.abstract: For Moldova's agriculture are characterized the existence of many small family farms and only a small number of corporate holdings (limited liabilities companies, agricultural production cooperatives etc). Most of individual farms, small by size produce only for own family consumption and cannot find their way to the market place. The accentuated poverty makes rural economy to flow more and more to a natural subsistence economy, isolating itself from the market economy. The goal of this paper is to delimitate different types of farms based on selected indicators and to appreciate their level of development. Differences in farms levels of development are appreciated through cluster analysis. The research includes the analysis of farms survey data. This research was carried as a part of the Academy of Sciences project "Sustainable rural development in Republic of Moldova in the context of EU accession". In the project were surveyed 938 individual farms from nine districts across the country. As a result, we distinguish three types of farms: natural, family and market household. The cluster analysis allows to characterize the farms level development, to determine the main priority directions, and to elaborate measures for the individual farms further sustainable development.

title: Institutional Reasoning: The Missing Capability of Financial Infrastructure

detail.title: Institutional Reasoning: The Missing Capability of Financial Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual study did not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Financial infrastructure has evolved to perform increasingly complex functions: transaction execution, settlement, record-keeping, compliance, and risk management. Yet despite these advances, contemporary infrastructure remains fundamentally execution-oriented. It verifies whether actions are valid, authorised, and technically feasible, but it rarely evaluates whether those actions preserve the long-term continuity of the institution itself.
This paper argues that financial infrastructure lacks a critical institutional capability: the ability to reason about the structural consequences of irreversible decisions before they are executed. It introduces the concept of institutional reasoning - the capability of infrastructure to evaluate how proposed actions affect institutional continuity, governance, ownership integrity, legal coherence, and decision-making capacity over time.
The paper distinguishes institutional reasoning from artificial intelligence, automation, compliance, and conventional decision support systems. Rather than replacing human judgment, institutional reasoning provides a structured architectural framework through which decision-makers can assess the long-term institutional implications of their choices before execution. In this sense, reasoning becomes an infrastructural capability rather than a computational feature.
Building on earlier work on institutional architecture and continuity as an institutional objective, the paper proposes that reasoning represents the next evolutionary capability of mature financial infrastructure. It outlines the architectural principles of a reasoning layer and argues that future infrastructure should be evaluated not only by its ability to execute transactions securely and efficiently, but also by its capacity to preserve institutional continuity through informed decision-making.
The paper concludes that embedding institutional reasoning into financial infrastructure is a necessary step in the evolution from execution-centred systems toward continuity-centred institutional architectures.

title: The Price of a Familiar Perspective
affiliations: and National Research University Higher School of Economics (Moscow) - National Research University Higher School of Economics (Perm)

detail.title: The Price of a Familiar Perspective
detail.abstract: A source becomes easier to use once one has learned how its perspective shapes what it says. We ask what that source-specific understanding is worth in a market for information. In a Gaussian model, familiarity accumulates at a diminishing rate and, for any proper prior about perspective, is most valuable at an intermediate level of expertise. Conditional on a one-sided consumption history, the better-understood provider charges more, serves more consumers, and earns more in a covered differentiated market. Two institutions that improve source understanding then have opposite effects: portable calibration information narrows the familiar provider's advantage, whereas post-consumption feedback about past outcomes widens it; within the interior market, both raise consumer surplus. A one-period extension shows that sufficiently cheap multihoming leaves the two providers equally well understood after that episode, so it creates no immediate familiarity advantage. The results isolate the ex post market value of understanding a source from habit or taste-based loyalty, and show why transparency can either weaken or reinforce an existing renewal advantage.

detail.abstract: According to the results of the 2025 execution of the enlarged government budget (EGB), revenue totaled Rb75.6 trillion, or 35.4% of GDP. In constant prices, year- over- year growth did not exceed 1%, and as a share of GDP, it was 0.3 percentage points (Table 2). Oil and gas revenues and non-oil and gas revenues amounted to Rb8.5 trillion and Rb67.1 trillion, respectively, or 4.0% and 31.4% of GDP. It should be noted that in 2025, oil and gas revenues hit a historic low of 4.0% of GDP. Given the positive growth in the EGB aggregate revenues, it is evident that the shortfall in resource rent revenues was fully offset by the growth in non-oil and gas revenues. The share of oil and gas revenues in the EGB revenue structure continues to decline — 11.2% in 2025 compared to 15.7% a year earlier — reflecting the trend toward reducing the budget’s dependence on natural resources. The federal budget’s share of total EGB revenue in 2025 fell to 49.4% from 51.7% in 2024.

title: Competition Between Local and National Restaurants in Farmington, New Mexico: A Microeconomic Analysis of Consumer Choice and Market Competition
affiliations: and

detail.title: Competition Between Local and National Restaurants in Farmington, New Mexico: A Microeconomic Analysis of Consumer Choice and Market Competition
detail.abstract: The restaurant industry is highly competitive, especially in communities where local businesses operate alongside national chains, and Farmington, New Mexico, provides a strong example of this dynamic. By comparing five national chains, Texas Roadhouse, McDonald’s, Taco Bell, Chili’s, and Olive Garden, with similar locally owned restaurants, this paper applies key microeconomic concepts such as monopolistic competition, product differentiation, economies of scale, and price elasticity of demand to understand how each type of business attracts customers. Data from menus, customer reviews, business websites, and pricing show that national chains often benefit from lower operating costs, brand recognition, and large-scale purchasing power, while local restaurants compete through unique menus, personalized service, regional specialties, and distinctive dining experiences. Overall, Farmington’s restaurant market illustrates how businesses with different strengths can successfully coexist within a monopolistically competitive industry.

title: Sea, Sand and Killer Robots: Towards a Caribbean Convention on AI Ethics and Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems

detail.title: Sea, Sand and Killer Robots: Towards a Caribbean Convention on AI Ethics and Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems
detail.abstract:
Since March 2025, drone strikes by Haitian security forces and the private military company Vectus Global have killed more than 1,200 people in Port-au-Prince, according to Human Rights Watch. This paper argues that the Caribbean is no longer a bystander to remote lethal force and that the arrival of artificial intelligence in these operations, whether through facial recognition targeting or autonomous decision-making, is a matter of time rather than speculation. Mexican cartels already deploy drones against civilians and soldiers, and the scholarly literature has flagged the specific risk of autonomous weapons migrating into the hands of insurgents and armed groups across the region.

The paper then posits a possible legal response. Haiti and Suriname are monist states, meaning ratified treaties become part of domestic law without further legislation. I test what I call the monist leapfrog hypothesis, the idea that this feature allows resource-poor states to acquire modern AI governance frameworks simply by acceding to a treaty. Drawing on comparative treaty scholarship and Haiti's own constitutional crisis, I conclude the hypothesis is limited in scope but has some value. Formal monism does not guarantee that courts apply treaties in practice, monism is not the same as self-execution, and a state without a functioning legislature cannot ratify anything at all, a problem Haiti currently faces.

 Haiti's existing acceptance of Inter-American Court jurisdiction gives it access to binding international oversight of the drone strikes, and a declaration under Article 12(3) of the Rome Statute could open a path to the International Criminal Court without new legislation. The paper closes by proposing  dedicated Caribbean and/or Latin American conventions regulating Artificial Intelligence and banning lethal autonomous weapons, built around regional enforcement and suggests borrowed frameworks from Europe may assist , and further argues that Trinidad and Tobago's incoming seat on the UN Security Council offers a real opportunity to advance it through diplomacy.

title: From Meter to Algorithm: An Empirical Analysis of Fare Estimation Discrepancies on Ride-Hailing Platforms and Their Impact on Taxi Demand

detail.title: From Meter to Algorithm: An Empirical Analysis of Fare Estimation Discrepancies on Ride-Hailing Platforms and Their Impact on Taxi Demand
detail.abstract: In recent years, the rise of ride-hailing apps has exerted substantial disruption on the traditional taxi industry. Both app-based ride-hailing services and conventional taxis mainly rely on platforms to obtain orders, but they differ in fare calculation and commission structures. Traditional taxis use metered pricing, whereas ride-hailing platforms estimate fares based on the driving trajectory. Regarding commission rules, traditional taxis face a per-trip commission capped at CNY 5 per ride, while ride-hailing platforms levy a proportional commission up to 30%. Drawing on theories of two-sided platforms and information asymmetry, the study argues that when trip fares exceed CNY 16.7, the platform has an incentive to adjust the relationship between estimated fares and final paid fares (in the case of ride-hailing) to maximize platform commission revenue. To test this proposition, this study collected paired observations by sending two researchers simultaneously on trips between fixed origin-destination pairs. I obtained 18 paired observations (36 trips in total) of ride-hailing and taxi rides and analyzed the data using paired t-tests. Several noteworthy findings emerged. On average, the estimated fare for ride-hailing was 2.6% lower than that for the taxi. The estimated fares exceeded actual paid fares by 5.4% for taxi. The actual fares paid for ride-hailing trips were 4.2% higher than the actual fares for taxi trips. All of these differences are statistically significant. By contrast, there was no significant difference between the ride-hailing platforms' estimated fares and the actual fares paid for raid-hailing trips. These findings enrich the literature on two-sided platforms and offer new empirical evidence on information asymmetry and platform governance in the urban passenger-transport market.

title: The Nature and Scope of Transboundary Obligations in Contemporary Climate Litigation
affiliations: and School of Law, Trinity College Dublin

detail.title: The Nature and Scope of Transboundary Obligations in Contemporary Climate Litigation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Martha Roggenkamp, Catherine Banet, Laura Kaschny, Odd Harald Wassenden eds. European Energy Law Report XVI, Intersentia, 2026

detail.abstract:
Recent jurisprudence in international, regional, and domestic courts treats Greenhouse Gases as a source of transboundary harm. Such treatment leads to findings of a global duty of care to be exercised by States and corporations, which creates obligations for cumulative and indirect harm, which are significantly broader than obligations to address direct or particular cross-border harm. The nature of such obligations has been mostly procedural – focusing on diligence and impact assessment obligations.

The idea of obligations for Scope 3 emissions have played an important role in the way transboundary obligations are understood. This idea broadens the temporal scope (ratione temporis) and territorial scope (ratione loci) of obligations. We argue that while the Dutch Shell case narrows the personal scope (ratione personae) of such obligations, the UK Finch case coupled with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) Court creates a presumptive obligation to include indirect and global emissions in impact assessments. Whether such procedural obligations translate into compensatory obligations is yet to be seen. In relation to compensatory obligations for adaptation costs, Lliuya v RWE creates a high evidentiary threshold, and European law appears to play a role in the Belgian farmer case in creating in-principle obligations for pro-rata adaptation costs.

detail.abstract:
Scientific research has traditionally relied on disciplinary methodologies that investigate specific empirical domains, while the overall process through which structural evidence evolves into cumulative scientific knowledge has remained largely fragmented. Observation, structural analysis, knowledge production, empirical evaluation, academic documentation, and scientific communication are typically addressed through independent practices rather than within a unified methodological architecture. This fragmentation limits methodological traceability, weakens cumulative knowledge development, and obscures the complete scientific lifecycle through which new scientific knowledge emerges.

This book introduces Dynamic Financial Applied Meta-Science (DFAS) as a constitutionally governed meta-scientific architecture designed to organize the entire progression from observable structural change to scientifically supported knowledge. Rather than replacing existing scientific disciplines or empirical research methods, DFAS provides a higher-order methodological system governing how structural transformations are identified, reconstructed, converted into candidate scientific knowledge, empirically evaluated, documented, communicated, and continuously refined within an integrated scientific ecosystem.

The volume establishes the philosophical foundations, scientific identity, methodological principles, constitutional structure, and scientific scope of DFAS. It presents the complete analytical architecture, including DFAS Signals, DFAS Path Signal Reports (DFAS-PSRs), DFAS Structural Synthesis Reports (DFAS-SSRs), DFAS Case Studies, the DFAS Law Validation Series, the DFAS Knowledge Production Protocol (DFAS-KPP), the DFAS Harvest Validation Protocol (DFAS-HVP), the DFAS Signal Harvest Repository, the Signal Harvest Series, and Path Architecture. Each component performs an independent constitutional function while remaining integrated within a transparent, evidence-based, and reproducible scientific workflow.

A defining contribution of DFAS is its constitutional separation of scientific functions. Knowledge production, methodological validation, empirical evaluation, academic documentation, scientific communication, and long-term scientific development are governed as distinct yet interconnected methodological domains. This organization strengthens methodological transparency, preserves evidence traceability, supports cumulative scientific development, and enables scientific knowledge to evolve through continuous empirical evaluation rather than isolated analytical outputs.

As the foundational volume of the DFAS framework, this work provides the conceptual and constitutional basis for a meta-scientific system intended to support the systematic production, organization, evaluation, documentation, and continuous development of structural knowledge across multiple domains of scientific inquiry.

title: Global Enterprise Value Report 2026 Edition

detail.title: Global Enterprise Value Report 2026 Edition
detail.abstract:
This report investigates a long-standing puzzle in corporate strategy and finance: why a small, persistent minority of publicly listed companies account for a disproportionate share of global enterprise value creation, while the large majority of otherwise comparable firms merely track or trail the broader market over long horizons. Evidence from roughly 300 globally significant companies across eleven industries and more than thirty countries, together with market-level data from the World Federation of Exchanges, PwC, the Fortune Global 500, the Forbes Global 2000, SIPRI, OECD and WIPO. The report develops and tests, to the extent current evidence allows, a capability-based explanation of enterprise value creation.
The central finding is that enterprise value is not adequately explained by any single financial variable, including revenue growth, profitability or return on invested capital in isolation. Instead, the evidence is most consistent with enterprise value behaving as an emergent property of an integrated capability system, comprising disciplined capital allocation, innovation productivity, operational excellence, customer economics, financial resilience, strategic adaptability and governance quality. Each capability reinforces the others through positive feedback over successive business cycles. This report formalises that proposition as the Enterprise Value Compounding Theory (EVCT™) and proposes a corresponding measurement framework, the Enterprise Value Compounding Index (EVCI™).
A small illustrative statistical analysis using real, sourced financial data for a handful of mega-cap companies finds no statistically significant relationship between return on invested capital and valuation multiple within that narrow, elite sample — a genuinely informative null result consistent with the report's broader thesis that no single metric, including ROIC, explains enterprise value once a company has already reached the frontier of capability. The report concludes that EVCT™ and EVCI™ constitute a well-evidenced, internally consistent research hypothesis rather than a fully validated predictive model, and specifies in detail the data architecture and out-of-sample validation required to complete that validation.

title: Strategy Uniqueness and Stock Price Crash Risk
affiliations: Michigan Technological University - College of Business and University of Massachusetts Dartmouth

detail.title: Strategy Uniqueness and Stock Price Crash Risk
detail.abstract: This paper examines how corporate strategy uniqueness influences stock price crash risk. Using portfolio analyses and panel regressions, we find that firms pursuing more unique strategies exhibit significantly lower crash risk. Channel analyses suggest that strategically unique firms face lower competitive pressure and weaker incentives to withhold bad news, thereby mitigating crash risk. Cross-sectional results further indicate that this negative relationship is stronger among firms with greater information asymmetry and weaker corporate governance. Overall, our findings provide important evidence on the role of corporate strategy in shaping firms' downside tail risk.

title:
From Transition to Transformation 
Why Moving Work Is Not the Same as Moving the Business Forwardand What Separates the Two

detail.title:
From Transition to Transformation 
Why Moving Work Is Not the Same as Moving the Business Forwardand What Separates the Two

detail.abstract:
Enterprises invest heavily in moving work — into Global Capability Centres (GCCs), Global Business Services (GBS) organizations, and shared services — yet the majority of these programs are measured, and often judged, on the wrong outcome. A transition that lands processes on time and on budget is frequently declared a success even when the underlying business is no more capable, resilient, or productive than before. In this paper I argue that transition and transformation are distinct disciplines. Transition relocates activity; transformation changes what the organization can do. The gap between them explains why so many well-executed moves still disappoint their sponsors.
Drawing on published research and my own experience across transitions and operating models, I examine why an estimated 70–88% of large-scale transformations fall short of their stated ambitions, and why lift and-shift moves that ignore leadership alignment, knowledge transfer, governance, culture, technology, and stabilization tend to plateau at cost arbitrage. I then introduce the Global Transition Readiness Framework — a structured way to assess whether an organization is prepared not merely to receive work, but to compound value from it. The paper closes with practical, executive-level recommendations, an honest statement of limitations, and directions for future research.

title: A Free-Energy Framework for Quantum Computing: A Physico-Economic Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Free-Energy Framework for Quantum Computing: A Physico-Economic Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper develops a **free-energy framework** for assessing the ultimate cost of quantum computing and argues that this cost is anchored in **available free energy**, not in qubit counts or computational metrics. We advance a four-step logical main thread that unifies the physico-economics of classical and quantum computing: (1) energy consumption and economic cost are of the same origin; (2) both are bound by the second law of thermodynamics (Landauer's $k_B T\ln 2$ floor); (3) a **reversal of cost location**—classical cost resides in the computation itself, whereas quantum cost resides in the macroscopic observation apparatus that must "see" the microscopic collapse; and (4) an anti-intuitive monotonicity—the finer the microscopic level spacing, the vaster the macroscopic enabling structure (cryogenic / vacuum / laser walls). Building on this, we give a **route-independent three-factor closure proof** showing that the free-energy lower bound of the observation apparatus is uniquely fixed by basic physical laws, and we back-fill the Standard-Quantum-Limit power factor with 2023–2026 medium-scale prototype data (a four-tier engineering-to-theory ladder from 300 W/qubit down to ~μW/qubit). We further provide a **precise fixed-capital model** comparing superconducting, ion-trap, and photonic routes and their Wright's-law decline curves. The honest endpoint: the true barrier of quantum computing is neither a physical free-energy floor (tiny but non-zeroable) nor "nearly free" marginal operation, but the **scarcity of the gigawatt-scale fixed capital** of a fault-tolerant machine.

title:
Team Success Gap (TSG) Theory

A Progressive Framework for Leadership Alignment, Role Clarity, and Organizational Success

detail.title:
Team Success Gap (TSG) Theory

A Progressive Framework for Leadership Alignment, Role Clarity, and Organizational Success
detail.abstract: Organizations depend on effective coordination between leaders and team members to achieve strategic objectives. Despite advances in organizational theory, many projects continue to fail because of unclear roles, weak leadership alignment, ineffective communication, and motivational imbalance. Traditional performance measurement systems often emphasize technical outputs while overlooking the dynamic relationship between leadership and team members. The Team Success Gap (TSG) Theory introduces a measurable framework for identifying, evaluating, and progressively reducing the invisible performance distance between leaders and their teams. This measurable distance is referred to as the Success Distance (x). The theory proposes that organizational effectiveness improves when this gap is continuously monitored and systematically reduced throughout the project lifecycle using the Progressive Gap Closure Scale (PGCS). TSG further integrates motivational and behavioral models including the Comprehensive Motivating Financial Model (CMFM), Self-Organizational Motivating Model (SOMM), Cognitive Evaluation Motivation Alignment Model (CEMAM), and Support and Comfort Crew Motivation (SCCM). The theory contributes to organizational behavior, administrative science, human resource management, and leadership studies by providing a practical model for measuring, correcting, and preventing leadership-team misalignment.

title: Does Identification Strategy Shape What We Find? A Structured Review and Design-Quality Appraisal of Forty Years of Expiration-Day Evidence

detail.abstract:
This article reviews forty years of empirical research on expiration-day effects in equity markets and asks a question the literature has not previously put to itself: whether what a study finds depends on how well it is identified. Twenty-six studies are synthesised, ten using Indian data and sixteen international comparators spanning nine other markets. Each is scored on a four-dimension design-quality instrument restricted to features observable in a published method section.

Three results emerge. First, the three classical expiration-day effects are not equally robust: abnormal volume is reported by nineteen of the twenty studies that test for it, elevated volatility by twenty of twenty-four, and price reversal by only fourteen of twenty. Second, studies exploiting an exogenous change in settlement regime report every one of the three effects less often than studies relying on descriptive comparison: 80.0 against 100.0 per cent for volume, 71.4 against 88.2 for volatility, and 57.1 against 76.9 for price reversal. This gradient is, however, statistically indistinguishable from chance in a corpus of this size, and identification strength is confounded with publication date; it is therefore reported as a hypothesis about the literature rather than a conclusion from it. Third, every Indian study published before 2025 is subject to a common identification failure: because the weekly expiry day was Thursday throughout, expiry day and calendar day are collinear and no estimator can separate a settlement effect from a day-of-week anomaly.

The article contributes a transparent design-quality instrument for this literature, the first evidence map of its accumulated findings, a formal statement of the collinearity problem, and a research agenda made feasible by the Indian regulatory reassignment of September 2025, within which the first study to exploit that reassignment is situated.

title: Inflation Uncertainty and Endogenous Planning Horizons
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Inflation Uncertainty and Endogenous Planning Horizons

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance and Economics Discussion Series, issue 2026-055, 2026[10.17016/FEDS.2026.055]

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: Finance & Economics Discussion Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We develop a finite-horizon planning model in which firms choose how far ahead to plan when setting prices. Planning further ahead improves a firm's pricing decision but requires cognitive effort. We derive analytical solutions for a firm's chosen planning horizon and show that large and persistent aggregate demand or supply disturbances induce firms to plan further ahead, making inflation more sensitive to shocks and generating endogenous movements in inflation uncertainty. Quantitatively, we show that the model matches the positive relationship between the size of inflation forecast revisions and inflation uncertainty observed in the data.

title: The Blue Pencil and the Severed Bargain - Severance of Contractual Terms under Sections 24, 27 and 57 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, with Comparative Common Law Perspectives
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Blue Pencil and the Severed Bargain - Severance of Contractual Terms under Sections 24, 27 and 57 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, with Comparative Common Law Perspectives
detail.abstract: This article examines the doctrine of blue pencil, the technique by which a court excises the offending words of a partly unlawful contract and enforces the lawful remainder. The question the article asks is where legitimate severance ends and impermissible reconstruction begins, and by what test the line is to be drawn. The method is doctrinal and comparative: the English origins are traced from Mitchel v Reynolds and Nordenfelt through Mason, Goldsoll and Attwood to the modern restatement in Tillman v Egon Zehnder; the Indian authorities are examined in the courts' own words, from Madhub Chunder and Chamarbaugwalla through Golikari, Krishan Murgai, Gujarat Bottling and Percept D'Mark to Shin Satellite, Beed District and Texco Marketing; the migration of the doctrine into arbitration is traced tier by tier, from the proviso to Section 34(2)(a)(iv) through J.G. Engineers, R.S. Jiwani, M. Hakeem and Trichy Thanjavur to the Constitution Bench in Gayatri Balasamy. The thesis defended is twofold: that the blue pencil is a subtractive jurisdiction whose legitimacy depends upon the refusal to reform, and that the phrase "to that extent" in Section 27 is itself a statutory blue pencil which Indian courts have correctly read through the lens of substantial severability rather than textual divisibility. The strongest objection, that severance is either arbitrary formalism or reformation in disguise, is stated and answered.

title: Online Bipartite Matching with Reusable Capacity under Non-Stationary Rewards
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School, Tsinghua University and Tsinghua University - Yau Mathematical Sciences Center

detail.title: Online Bipartite Matching with Reusable Capacity under Non-Stationary Rewards
detail.abstract: We study online bipartite matching with reusable server capacity and non-stationary rewards. Jobs arrive sequentially, reveal compatible servers, reward rates, and processing durations, and must be accepted or rejected irrevocably. An accepted job occupies one unit of server capacity only during its processing interval, so an assignment may displace an unknown sequence of future jobs. Existing guarantees are typically calibrated by a global reward range, which can become arbitrarily large when rewards drift over a long horizon. We instead impose a locally bounded reward condition: reward rates of jobs that can compete for the same server within a relevant time window differ by at most a factor $\delta$. Under this condition, we develop two BALANCE-type algorithms with time-aware opportunity-cost losses. TS-BAL maximizes cumulative blocking losses over feasible reuse schedules and achieves a competitive ratio of $2\ln(\delta D)+\mathcal O(\ln\ln(\delta\vee D))$. GR-BAL uses a greedy relaxation of this loss and achieves $\ln(\delta D)+\mathcal O(\ln\ln(\delta\vee D))$, matching a lower bound of $\ln(\delta D)$ in the leading term. Numerical experiments demonstrate robust performance under substantial global reward drift and favorable finite-capacity performance.

title: Cross-Training for Correlated Crew Absence

detail.title: Cross-Training for Correlated Crew Absence
detail.abstract: Cross-training can protect production coverage when absent workers leave skill-specific gaps, but absences are often correlated within crews. This paper studies how a fixed secondaryskill budget should be allocated when crew-level shocks are possible. A transparent synthetic benchmark contains 24 workers, six task skills, four crews, and 20 required task units per shift. Each worker has one primary skill and at most one added skill. A scenario-greedy portfolio is trained on correlated absence draws; exact bipartite assignment then measures held-out coverage. The comparison includes specialists, random links, a skill chain, and a demand-only rule. On 4000 common test scenarios, the shock-aware portfolio lowers mean unmet work from 1.782 to 0.777 task units, a 56.4% reduction, and raises the full-coverage rate from 29.6% to 69.4%. Its advantage over the skill chain is smaller:-0.045 task units per shift (95% interval [-0.052,-0.038]; paired d z =-0.187). When marginal absence is held fixed, increasing crew-shock probability reduces the relative value of cross-training because a larger share of shortage is caused by insufficient present headcount rather than skill mismatch. The contribution is a reproducible decomposition of headcount shortage and skill-mismatch shortage, together with a transparent protocol for evaluating sparse training portfolios before personnel-level implementation.

title: Diplomacy without Reconciliation: Affective Acknowledgement, Recognized Loss, and the Political Receivability of Adversarial Bargains
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.abstract:
Why are materially advantageous diplomatic offers sometimes rejected as submission, while visible losses remain politically receivable as legitimate compromise? Material bargaining, coercive leverage, domestic audience response, attraction, face management, recognition, and emotional performance each explain part of this puzzle, but none specifies when an adversarial bargain can be publicly taken up as an authored option by those expected to live under it. Building on Emotional Sovereignty and the Affective Uptake Condition (AUC), this article develops affective acknowledgement as a relational condition under which offers can function politically as reasons for particular publics, not as an emotional rival to rational bargaining. It makes seven contributions. First, it translates AUC into international negotiation without attributing a mind or emotion to a state. Second, it defines affective acknowledgement and its hostile-setting minimum, passive acknowledgement. Third, it identifies diplomatic affective inversion: benefit can be rejected under domination, whereas visible loss can remain receivable under acknowledged authorship. Fourth, it formulates a recognized-loss proposition with strict exclusions for deception, existential coercion, rights violations, and irreversible subordination.
Fifth, it specifies coercive beneficence and a designer-enforcer-evaluator structure of external affective capture in which the same actor also benefits from its own interpretation of elicited compliance. Sixth, it distinguishes unequal capabilities from equality of addressability. Seventh, it establishes a capture boundary separating genuine grievance from manufactured uptake. A concept-forming design translates five noncompensatory conditions into observable traces and refutation tests. Structured illustrations and boundary probes from U.S.–China diplomacy, the Iran nuclear file, the INF Treaty, and Ukrainian and Russian wartime cases generate plausibility, not causal estimates. The outcome is political receivability, not agreement, approval, justice, or post-agreement durability.

title: Rule Rent: A Concealed Competitive Logic in Global Economic and Trade Governance

detail.title: Rule Rent: A Concealed Competitive Logic in Global Economic and Trade Governance
detail.abstract: Global green economic and trade rules face a structural misalignment: the actors with the strongest green production capacity tend to have the weakest voice in rule-making, while those who dominate rule-making are experiencing a relative decline in their production and cost advantages. This paper introduces the concept of "rule rent" to uncover the mechanism generating this misalignment. Rule rent refers to the systematic benefits that actors continuously extract from global economic and trade flows by controlling the power to define rules, the power to certify compliance, the power to adjudicate disputes, and the power to govern financial channels-without directly engaging in production-based competition. In contrast, "capability-based competition" rests on actual construction efficiency, manufacturing strength, and cost advantages. The systematic tilting of rule rent over capability-based competition constitutes the deep driving force behind the structural decoupling between nominal rules and actual capabilities in global economic and trade governance. The paper delineates the four power components of rule rent and its closed-loop effect, and establishes its analytical boundaries in dialogue with theories of rent-seeking, structural power, and regulatory rent. It then illustrates the operational features of rule rent through concrete practices in the green economy and trade domain, analyzes the structural asymmetry between these two logics of competition, and concludes by discussing institutional directions for compressing the space of rule rent.

title: Technical Arbitrariness in Regulated Selection Processes: A Diagnostic Framework

detail.title: Technical Arbitrariness in Regulated Selection Processes: A Diagnostic Framework

detail.abstract: Regulated selection processes—public employment, bank licensing, risk model validation, compliance certification—frequently rest on technical standards whose operational content is not defined ex ante. This paper defines technical arbitrariness as substantive technical decisions issued without published criteria, without standardized methodology, without enforceable technical reasoning, and without effective contradiction mechanisms. The framework is grounded in the documentary analysis of a Peruvian case—CAS Selection Process No. 804-2020-CG, closed by SERVIR Report No. 000879-2021-SERVIR-GDSRH—and, as a distinctive feature, in the formal and methodological reading of the applicant's own working paper: a function-by-function equivalence matrix anchored in the International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing and the COSO 2013 Framework. The paper formalizes the matrix as a coverage index, subjects it to critical methodological evaluation against internal audit quality assurance standards, and traces its fate through the three institutional instances that received it without substantively evaluating it. Four regulatory gaps are identified, and three regulatory reforms are proposed, whose transferability is examined against community banking supervision under FDICIA §112, model risk management under Fed SR 11-7, and BSA/AML compliance. The paper concludes that technical arbitrariness is a structural property of ambiguous standards, correctable through regulatory design.

title: Can Human Behaviour Reveal Cultural Preferences? Introducing the Behavioural Information Request Framework (BIRF) through Voluntary QR-Code Interactions
affiliations: University of Warsaw

detail.title: Can Human Behaviour Reveal Cultural Preferences? Introducing the Behavioural Information Request Framework (BIRF) through Voluntary QR-Code Interactions
detail.abstract: Measuring genuine human engagement in cultural environments remains challenging because conventional approaches primarily rely on questionnaires, interviews, direct observation, or technologyintensive sensing systems that may interrupt natural visitor behaviour. This study introduces the Behavioural Information Request Framework (BIRF), a new behavioural measurement framework that captures revealed information-seeking behaviour through voluntary QR-code interactions. The framework was implemented during a seven-day live sculpture exhibition comprising 33 sculptures at the Academy of Fine Arts, Kolkata. Five sculptures were randomly selected for empirical analysis and equipped with Behavioural Information Request Points (BIRPs), allowing visitors to voluntarily request philosophical, material, or price information using their own smartphones. Each voluntary interaction automatically generated an anonymous Behavioural Information Request Event (BIRE), which was recorded with a timestamp in a cloud-based database without collecting personally identifiable information. The resulting scan logs were systematically transformed into four research-ready behavioural datasets. Visitor behaviour was analysed using descriptive statistics, Poisson regression, binary logistic regression, and K-means clustering. The results show that visitor engagement increased significantly with the number of sculptures explored. Visitors exploring more sculptures were significantly more likely to request both philosophical and price information. Behavioural segmentation further identified four distinct visitor groups: Casual Visitors, Knowledge Seekers, Potential Buyers, and Highly Engaged Explorers. These findings demonstrate that voluntary QR-code interactions provide meaningful behavioural evidence that can be transformed into robust quantitative datasets without questionnaires or researcher intervention. The proposed framework offers a simple, low-cost, privacy-preserving, and scalable methodology for measuring revealed cultural preferences and visitor engagement. Beyond sculpture exhibitions, the framework can be applied to museums, galleries, cultural heritage sites, libraries, educational institutions, science centres, tourism attractions, and other public environments requiring unobtrusive behavioural measurement.

detail.abstract: The article resolves the scholarly problem of establishing the conditions under which an attack on a merchant vessel during an international armed conflict qualifies as a war crime and, at the same time, as an act of aggression against the flag State and the coastal State. The topical relevance is prompted by the practice of July 2026 in the Black, Azov and Caspian Seas, when dozens of vessels flying the flags of States not party to the conflict were subjected to the use of force, and third States advanced claims against both belligerents. The methodological basis is the testing of a hypothesis by attempted refutation: the conditions under which a vessel forfeits the protection of a civilian object are examined separately, and only thereafter is the final qualification formulated. The article applies the formal-legal, comparative-legal and systemic-structural methods, together with the method of interpretation under Articles 31 and 32 of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. It is established that an attack on a vessel which does not meet the criteria of a military objective under paragraph 2 of Article 52 of Additional Protocol I of 1977, and does not fall within paragraphs 60 or 67 of the 1994 San Remo Manual, engages the offences under Article 8(2)(b)(i), (ii) and (iv) of the Rome Statute and constitutes an act of aggression under Article 3(d) of United Nations General Assembly Resolution 3314 (XXIX) and Article 8 bis (2)(d) of the Rome Statute. It is demonstrated that a vessel's sanctions listing, its carriage of hydrocarbons, or its membership of the socalled shadow fleet do not in themselves convert the vessel into a military objective, since sanctions are an economic and not a military instrument. It is substantiated that a State attack on a vessel does not amount to piracy, owing to the absence of the element of private ends under Article 101 of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that the 1988 Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts against the Safety of Maritime Navigation does not apply to the actions of armed forces in armed conflict, by virtue of the exception in paragraph 2 of Article 2 bis of the 2005 Protocol thereto. A distinction is drawn between the interdiction of a sanctioned vessel as a law-enforcement measure and an attack upon it as an act of hostilities. The claim of States' tacit endorsement of an expanded notion of military objective is refuted. The scholarly novelty lies in the formulation of a single qualification test, applicable irrespective of which party to the conflict carried out the attack, and in its testing against the material of the events of July 2026.

title: A Simulation Analytics Framework for System-Level Digital Twins in Hospital Operations
affiliations: University of Quebec at Montreal (UQAM), Universite du Quebec a Montreal, Universite du Quebec a Montreal and University of Quebec at Montreal (UQAM) - Université du Québec à Montréal

detail.title: A Simulation Analytics Framework for System-Level Digital Twins in Hospital Operations
detail.abstract: Digital twins in healthcare have predominantly focused on object-level applications, including personalized medicine, organ twins, and wearable-based patient monitoring, whereas system-level digital twins that support the planning and operation of healthcare facilities remain largely unexplored. This study addresses this gap by proposing a revised typology of healthcare digital twins and developing a system-level digital twin for hospital operations. The proposed typology integrates the healthcare facility life cycle with an analytics framework that combines descriptive and diagnostic analytics while introducing a prospective analytics dimension to support simulation-based what-if analyses. The digital twin was developed for a multiservice ambulatory care center within the CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l'Île-de-Montréal, Canada, integrating blood collection, screening, medical examinations, and vaccination services. A hybrid agent-based and discrete-event simulation model was developed in AnyLogic using service-time and arrival estimates derived from field observations, managerial input, and clinical expert consultation. Six operational scenarios involving alternative staffing levels and service durations were evaluated using 500 simulation replications per scenario. The proposed typology comprises twelve categories, seven of which are represented by previously reported healthcare digital twins, while the presented application occupies the system-level design category. The baseline configuration proved operationally infeasible, with an average patient length of stay of 266 minutes and service completion extending to 01:29. Improving staffing or service durations individually was insufficient to achieve acceptable operational performance. In contrast, jointly optimizing staffing and service durations reduced the mean patient length of stay to 75 minutes and enabled completion of daily operations by 19:14, representing a 3.5-fold improvement over the baseline. These findings demonstrate that system-level digital twins can provide actionable analytics for healthcare facility planning by enabling the evaluation of operational alternatives before implementation, while the proposed typology offers a structured framework for classifying and comparing healthcare digital twins across the healthcare facility life cycle.

detail.abstract: According to Our Finding, Scheme acts as an instant tonic.Where Policy acts as a complete medicine for a Commoners.This paper critically examines the paradoxical dynamics between economic "schemes" and "policies,"challenging the growing preference for short-term,welfare-based initiatives over long-term,structural policy frameworks in contemporary governance.The study conceptualizes schemes as a "tonic" that provides instant but often ephemeral relief, while policies are positioned as "medicine" that offers sustainable, comprehensive solutions to economic ailments.This paper demonstrates that schemes generate high nominal benefits but impose significant fiscal burdens,opportunity costs, inflationary pressures, and potential disincentives to productive work.In contrast, policies create multidimensional multiplier effects that enhance real economic variables,generate sustainable employment, and promote long-term development.The analysis incorporates budget data from welfare schemes,including west bengal's "Lakshmir Bhandar" program, and fiscal documents to substantiate claims regarding fiscal deficits, public debt, and welfare trade-offs.The paper argues that while schemes may be appropriate for crisis situations or targeted support to marginalized communities,their universal and politically-driven expansion without adequate cost-benefit analysis leads to welfare losses, fiscal instability, and neglect of critical infrastructure (Like:Hospital,Electricity Connection,Pure tap water connection, School/College/University,SEZ,R&D,Research hub,Trade & commerce,trasport & communication, manufacturing units as well as maintain Law and order & so on) and human development investments.The Paper illustrate how unchecked scheme allocation can trigger Diminish real purchasing power, encourage leisure over productive labour, Crowding Out essential for long term development policy.Drawing on analogical reasoning-including the mother-father dichotomy of rule-based versus discretionary policy-the research highlights the urgent need for transparent cost accounting, evidence-based policy-making, and a reorientation toward productive, sustainable economic interventions. Ultimately, the paper advocates for a paradigm shift from scheme-centric populism to policy-driven sustainability, emphasizing that the true measure of good governance lies not in how much is distributed, but in how much is built for the future.

title: Structural Repositioning of Political Actors under the Constraints of the Strategic Environment: An Interpretive Framework for Negotiation Breakthroughs in the Cairo Talks Analytical Study in Light of Geopolitical Transformations and Transitional Governance

detail.title: Structural Repositioning of Political Actors under the Constraints of the Strategic Environment: An Interpretive Framework for Negotiation Breakthroughs in the Cairo Talks Analytical Study in Light of Geopolitical Transformations and Transitional Governance
detail.abstract:
This study investigates the structural factors that explained the negotiation breakthrough witnessed in the Cairo talks following the war on the Gaza Strip. It proceeds from the hypothesis that this breakthrough was not the result of the emergence of new negotiation approaches or unilateral changes in the positions of Palestinian actors, but rather stemmed essentially from the transformations that affected the strategic environment surrounding the political process, and the consequent structural repositioning within Palestinian actors. The study begins from the central problematic of political and negotiation deadlock that characterized the previous phase, which limited the ability of Palestinian parties to produce a coherent political stance-one supported by Arab actors and capable of interacting with the challenges imposed by Israeli objectives and regional and international variables. Accordingly, the study focuses on analyzing how Fatah and Hamas responded to this changing environment, and how each redefined its institutional functions and political priorities within the context of transitional arrangements and the post-war phase.
The study employs Indicator-Based Analysis within the framework of Functional and Engineering Dissection Analysis (FEDA), grounded in the theoretical foundation of Sovereign Stability Theory (SST). It analyzes five principal levels: international legal transformations; reconstruction and transitional governance arrangements; Egypt’s regional role as organizer of the transitional environment; the Israeli determinant as a factor shaping the security and geographic domain; and the structural transformations within Fatah and Hamas alongside competing functional approaches. The study concludes that the negotiation breakthrough was not the product of the victory of a single political approach, but rather the result of a redistribution of functions and roles within a strategic environment that redefined the conditions of political effectiveness. Fatah experienced structural repositioning toward the requirements of institutional governance and management of the transitional phase, while Hamas revealed a reordering of centers of influence toward leadership more connected to the negotiation track and the regional environment. Competing functional approaches did not disappear; rather, their roles were redefined within a formula more integrated with the requirements of the new phase. The study proposes that explaining Palestinian transformations after the war requires moving from analyzing isolated political positions to analyzing the environment that reshapes actors’ choices, where the ability to generate functional stability and manage the transitional phase has become one of the fundamental determinants of political effectiveness.

title: War Risk Premiums and the Indian Pharmaceutical Supply Chain: Assessing the Economic Implications of Geopolitical Disruptions

detail.title: War Risk Premiums and the Indian Pharmaceutical Supply Chain: Assessing the Economic Implications of Geopolitical Disruptions
